The Blue-and-yellow tanager (Rauenia bonariensis) is a passerine species whose early developmental stages have been characterised through observational studies of captive broods. Neonates emerge with a relatively modest initial body mass; freshly hatched chicks typically weigh between 3.4 and 4 grams, with a reported mean hatchling mass of 3.8 grams [Ww0 = 3.8 grams]. This low birth weight situates the species among the smaller-bodied tanagers at the point of hatching. The altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning during the first days of life, and their growth trajectory from this minimal starting point appears to be rapid under standard rearing conditions.

As the nestling period progresses, the developing chicks undergo a phase of rapid mass gain that culminates in a distinctive size dimorphism between the sexes at adulthood. Field measurements of reproductively mature individuals indicate that adult females attain an ultimate wet weight of 37 grams [Wwi = 37 grams], while adult males reach a somewhat smaller asymptotic mass of 32 grams [Wwi = 32 grams]. This roughly 15% difference in body mass between the sexes is a notable feature of the species' life history and likely reflects differential energetic investments associated with egg production in females versus male-male competition for territories and mates.
